🎯 Objectives
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
- Understand what the first conditional expresses.
- Form sentences with "if" + present simple and "will" + base verb.
- Put the two clauses in either order with correct punctuation.
- Use the first conditional to talk about real future possibilities.

🔍 Warm-up
Read: "If you study hard, you will pass the exam." This sentence has a condition (if you study hard) and a result (you will pass). It talks about a real, possible future. This is the first conditional.

I. What the first conditional is for
📘 Rule (functions)
We use the first conditional to talk about a REAL and POSSIBLE situation in the future and its result. It answers "What will happen IF ...?"
- If it rains, we will stay at home.
- If you help me, I will finish quickly.
The situation is possible, not imaginary. It is likely to happen.

👀 Note
The first conditional is often used for warnings, promises, offers and predictions:
- If you touch that, you will hurt yourself. (warning)
- If you come with me, I will show you the way. (offer)

II. The form
📘 Rule (structure)
The first conditional has TWO parts (clauses):
1. The "if" clause = the condition → present simple.
2. The main clause = the result → will + base verb.
📏 Form
If + subject + present simple , subject + will + base verb.
- If I have time, I will call you.
- If she studies, she will pass.

✏️ Worked examples
- If the weather is nice, we will go to the beach.
- If you don't hurry, you will miss the bus.
- If he practises every day, he will improve.

⚠️ The golden rule
NEVER use "will" in the "if" clause. The condition stays in the present simple.
Wrong: If it will rain, we will stay home.
Right: If it rains, we will stay home.

III. Word order and punctuation
📘 Rule
The two clauses can come in either order. The meaning is the same.
📏 Two orders
1. If clause first → use a comma between the clauses.
- If you are tired, you will sleep well.
2. Main clause first → no comma.
- You will sleep well if you are tired.

🛠️ Method: building a first conditional sentence
Step 1 — Find the condition (the "if" part) and put it in the present simple.
Step 2 — Find the result and put it in "will + base verb".
Step 3 — Decide the order. If the "if" clause comes first, add a comma.
Step 4 — Check: no "will" after "if".

✏️ Worked examples (both orders)
- If we leave now, we will arrive on time.
- We will arrive on time if we leave now.
- If you eat too much, you will feel ill.
- You will feel ill if you eat too much.

IV. Variations and useful details
📘 Rule (other results)
The result clause can use other modal or command forms instead of "will":
- can: If you finish early, you can go out.
- may / might (less certain): If it is sunny, we might have a picnic.
- imperative (advice or instruction): If you feel tired, take a rest.
✏️ Worked examples
- If you need help, you can ask the teacher.
- If you see Sami, tell him to call me.

📘 Rule (unless)
"unless" means "if ... not". It introduces a condition of exception.
- I will not go unless you come with me. (= if you do not come)
- Unless you study, you will not pass.

✏️ Worked paragraph
Next Saturday my class is planning a trip to the mountains. If the weather is good, we will leave early in the morning. If we take the bus, we will save money. Our teacher says that if everyone brings food, we will have a great picnic. But if it rains, we will visit the museum instead. I am sure we will have fun if we all work together.

⚠️ Common mistakes
1. "will" in the if clause: If you will come → If you come.
2. Wrong tense in the result: If you study, you pass → you will pass.
3. Missing comma when the if clause is first, or adding one when it is second.
4. Confusing "unless" (= if not) and adding another "not": Unless you don't study → Unless you study.
5. Using "would" (that is the second conditional, a different lesson).

⭐ Recap
- First conditional = real, possible future situation and its result.
- Form: If + present simple, ... will + base verb.
- Never use "will" in the "if" clause.
- Either order is fine; use a comma only when the "if" clause comes first.
- Results can also use can, may, might or the imperative; "unless" means "if not".

📘 Language bank
Structure words: if, unless, will, won't, can, might.
Result verbs: pass, fail, miss, arrive, finish, improve, help, feel.
Useful sentences: If you study hard, you will pass the exam. / If it rains, we will stay at home. / You will miss the bus if you don't hurry. / If you need help, you can ask me. / Unless you leave now, you will be late.

📝 Practice
Exercise 1 — Complete the first conditional.
1. If it (rain) ______ , we (stay) ______ at home.
2. If you (study) ______ hard, you (pass) ______ the exam.
3. If we (not / hurry) ______ , we (miss) ______ the bus.
4. She (be) ______ happy if she (win) ______ the prize.

Exercise 2 — Correct the mistake.
1. If it will rain, we will stay home.
2. If you study, you pass the exam.
3. If you will help me, I will finish quickly.
4. Unless you don't hurry, you will be late.

Exercise 3 — Finish the sentences with your own ideas.
1. If I have free time this weekend, ...
2. If it is sunny tomorrow, ...
3. I will be very happy if ...

✅ Answers
Exercise 1: 1. rains ... will stay 2. study ... will pass 3. don't hurry ... will miss 4. will be ... wins.
Exercise 2: 1. If it rains, we will stay home. 2. If you study, you will pass the exam. 3. If you help me, I will finish quickly. 4. Unless you hurry, you will be late.

🗣️ Speaking task
Play a chain game. One student starts: "If I go to the shop, I will buy some fruit." The next continues: "If I buy some fruit, I will make a salad." Keep the chain going around the class.

👀 Extra note
The single most important rule: NEVER use "will" after "if". The condition stays in the present simple.
- Right: If it rains, we will stay home.
- Wrong: If it will rain...
And use a comma only when the "if" clause comes first.

🌍 Real-life English
The first conditional is the language of real choices. Parents use it ("If you finish your homework, you can watch TV"), coaches use it ("If we train hard, we will win"), and you use it every time you plan around a condition ("If it is sunny, I will go to the beach; if it rains, I will stay at home"). Try finishing five sentences that start with "If..." about your own week, always keeping the present simple after "if" and "will" in the result. This structure lets you talk about all the possible futures that depend on what you decide to do.

📋 Summary
- First conditional talks about a real, possible future situation and its result.
- Form: If + subject + present simple , subject + will + base verb.
- Golden rule: never use "will" in the if-clause — the condition stays in the present simple.
- Word order: comma after the if-clause when it comes first; no comma when the main clause comes first.
- Result clause can also use can (permission), may/might (less certain), or the imperative (advice).
- "unless" means "if ... not": Unless you study, you will not pass = If you don''t study, you will not pass.
- Typical uses: warnings, promises, offers, predictions about the future.
- Common mistakes: "If you will come" (wrong) → "If you come" (right); missing "will" in the result clause.
- Quick check: is the situation possible and about the future? Then it is a first conditional.
